The liquidity table therefore shows the commitment less borrowings at 2026-09-30, which is before letters of credit, and no figure for 2023-12-31. Letters of credit outstanding would close it. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 120; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 128; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25 - Medium: The issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is derived from income before tax, interest expense, bank fees and other, and amortization of intangible assets. Interest income on client funds stays inside it, and the interim ratios rest on a last-twelve-months construction with no statement tie. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 12; calculation C01; calculation C02 - Medium: The quarterly reports print no debt note, so instrument carrying values, issuance costs and rates at 2026-09-30 are not stated, and the USD 4 million difference between note principal and balance-sheet debt is unexplained. The annual note gives 5 of issuance costs at 2025-12-31, which suggests the cause but does not prove it. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 118; calculation C19 - High: The revolver's security, rank and guarantors, and the identity of its borrower, are not stated in the sources, and the note guarantors are not named, so the debt stack shows the two note issues only and excludes the revolver, which has no balance. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 119; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134 - Medium: The statements print dashes that are carried as not supplied, not as zero: accounts receivable in FY2025, other payroll assets in FY2025, accounts payable and other liabilities in FY2024 and 9M 2025, workers' compensation in 9M 2025, proceeds from sale of business in three periods, other investments in two years, the 2031 note proceeds and revolver proceeds outside FY2023, dividends in FY2023, revolver repayment in 9M 2026, investments in FY2024 and FY2025, and the transaction and integration costs and restructuring lines. Operating cash flow still equals the printed adjustments and movements in every period, and the 2024 annual report's two payables lines net to zero for FY2024. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 100–101 - Low: Lines printed in the annual statements but not in the interim statements (other payroll assets, accrued health insurance costs, acquisition of subsidiary in annual columns, financing items in 9M columns) are shown as not printed, and the interim balance sheet does not print the revolver or noncurrent investment lines. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29 - Medium: The 2025 quarterly reports were not supplied, so discrete 2025 quarters and a balance sheet at 2025-09-30 are not available as filed, the 2026 reports say some prior-year amounts were reclassified, and no maintenance or growth capital expenditure split is printed. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95 - Low: The company reports one segment, so no segment revenue or elimination schedule exists; revenue is shown by service type, and no segment sum is stated. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 42 - Low: The first quarter report gives April 8, 2026 as the closing day of the Cocoon acquisition and the later reports give April 10, 2026; the cash price of USD 22 million net of cash acquired is in the 9M 2026 investing flows and the day does not change any figure here. Basis: 10-Q_2026-03-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-06-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 43; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29 - Low: The 2024 annual report prints the FY2023 Adjusted EBITDA margin as 14.2% and the 2025 annual report prints 14.0% for the same USD 697 million; the margin used here is recomputed from printed revenue. Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; calculation C21 - Low: The October dividend is linked to the USD 13 million declared and unpaid at 2026-09-30 by inference, and its day is not stated, so it is held in the post-balance-sheet table with no date. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25 - Medium: The 2025 annual report merges payables, impairment and other lines that the 2024 annual report prints separately, and the nine-month interim statements print Other where the annual statements print impairment of intangibles and other; totals agree, but line-level trends across annual and interim columns are not like for like. Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 100–101; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29

facts.text: Overall, Trinet presents medium sponsor and governance risk. The key supported behavior is a debt-funded repurchase of USD 1,000 million in 2023, including USD 360 million bought from the largest stockholder, which matters because it raised leverage and set the 2031 maturity and implies that the board will lever for repurchases when it judges the price right. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Debt service capacity is strong and the maturity profile is clean, but the first test is the sequence of refinancing. Net debt of USD 568 million is 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA of USD 359 million, or USD 581 million and 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, and cash interest cover is 7.33x. Both notes are fixed rate and senior unsecured, and the first maturity is USD 500 million in March 2029. The USD 700 million revolver has no borrowings but matures in August 2028, before those notes, so it must be extended or replaced to remain a backstop when the notes turn current; its maturity date is stated only in the 2024 annual report. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Revenue durability is weak because the client base is shrinking and can leave on short notice. Total worksite employees were 10.99% below a year earlier at 2026-09-30, mainly in technology and professional services clients and partly because of health benefit repricing, and total revenues fell 4.86% in the nine months despite 8% higher monthly revenue per worksite employee. Clients can generally cancel on 30 days' notice, and five states account for about 64% of paid wages, which concentrates both revenue and insurance pricing. No client exceeded 10% of revenue in 2023 to 2025 and bad debt was USD 3 million a year, so the risk is broad attrition, not the loss of one large client. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: A material part of reported EBITDA is yield on client funds, and it is running off. Interest income was 19.76% of FY2025 reported EBITDA and 14.76% over the last twelve months, and it fell to USD 39 million in the nine months to 2026-09-30 from USD 53 million because refund interest and average balances fell. Receivables from the IRS for employee retention credits fell from USD 831 million at FY2024 to USD 310 million at 2026-09-30, so part of the shrinking client balances is refunds being processed, not clients leaving, which qualifies the Financial foundation's reading of the fall as a shrinking funding float; the filings do not say how much. If the IRS finds claims ineligible, Trinet may seek reimbursement from clients, to whom a net USD 21 million had been distributed at 2026-09-30, but the annual report says the IRS holds professional employer organizations responsible for repaying rejected tax credits and a contract does not guarantee recovery from clients. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest case against the earnings concern is the 2026 recovery: nine-month operating cash flow was USD 317 million against USD 242 million, the insurance cost ratio was 86% against 90%, management calls the reset of health benefit rates substantially complete, and net debt was 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA against 1.79x at FY2025, with USD 581 million and 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend. If the ratio holds between 86% and 89% for four more quarters while worksite employees stabilise, earnings stability would move from weak to average and leverage would fall without a change in policy. The case is weaker than it looks: the nine-month ratio includes the USD 21 million one-time recovery, the third quarter ratio was 89%, USD 43 million of the USD 75 million rise in operating cash flow came from smaller working-capital outflows that can reverse, and the client base was still 10.99% smaller than a year earlier. facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: The strongest support is low, fixed-rate leverage with a distant first maturity. Net debt of USD 568 million is 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, or USD 581 million and 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, all debt is two unsecured fixed-rate notes, and the first maturity is USD 500 million in March 2029. facts.label: Margin resilience
facts.text: Margins are fragile to claims experience and only partly flexible on cost. Insurance costs were USD 3,835 million of USD 4,793 million total costs and expenses in FY2025, and because fees are set ahead of claims a rise in the insurance cost ratio falls straight through to earnings, as the move from 84% to 91% did. The Adjusted EBITDA margin fell from about 14% in FY2023 to 8.48% in FY2025 and was 9.53% over the last twelve months; the FY2023 margin is printed as 14.2% in one annual report and 14.0% in the other. Operating expenses of USD 902 million carry the cost flexibility: restructuring costs of USD 49 million in 2024, USD 11 million in 2025 and USD 13 million in nine months 2026 show that management can resize costs, but savings are not quantified, so margin recovery rests mainly on repricing and claims, not cost. facts.label: Outlook
facts.text: Over three to five years the credit is a question of policy and refinancing. USD 500 million falls due in March 2029 and USD 400 million in August 2031, and a refinancing of the 2029 notes at a higher coupon would raise interest cost. With moderate leverage and free cash flow, refinancing capacity looks adequate if earnings hold, but it will depend on the leverage the board allows through buybacks, the insurance cost ratio and the worksite employee trend at the time. facts.text: The issuer-specific downside is a claims shock layered on continued client losses. The initiating condition is health utilisation above the rates fixed for the plan year, as in 2024 and 2025, and the first operational break is the insurance cost ratio rising while worksite employees keep falling, because fees cannot be reset until the next benefit period. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Trinet presents an adequate business profile supported by scale in small-business HR outsourcing, with total revenues of USD 5,010 million in FY2025, an operating record since 1988 and prefunded client money, but credit quality is constrained by an insurance-spread earnings base, a shrinking client base and shareholder payments at the level of free cash flow. No peer set was supplied, so the comparison with typical leveraged-credit issuers in the sector is not established. Cash-flow durability appears adequate for debt service, because capital spending is modest and debt is low and fixed rate, but weak as a measure of recurring earnings, because the insurance cost ratio and client losses can remove a large share of EBITDA within a year. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the insurance cost ratio and worksite employee trend at the time, the leverage the board allows through buybacks, and the extension of the revolver before it matures in August 2028. The primary downside path is claims costs rising above rates set in advance while clients leave, with cash drawn into carrier collateral and shareholder payments continuing. Further analysis would require the credit agreement and indentures, the covenant level, letters of credit outstanding, the proxy statement, a peer set and market quotes. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: the insurance cost ratio. ## Request

Source readiness for Trinet Group, Inc. (tnet-937098) as of 2026-11-18 under the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is whether the five supplied filings can support the financial foundation, business and governance and fundamental credit work selected for this run, and what the filings cannot support. No ratings, quotes, deal terms, peer set, portfolio or executed legal documents were supplied.
## Sources

Document dates are the dates on each report's signature page; the 2025 annual report (filed 2026-02-12) and the June 2026 quarterly report (filed 2026-07-30) are also confirmed by the September 2026 quarterly report. No earlier analyses were supplied and no external sources were used. The run settings are not issuer evidence and are not listed.
## Findings
### Bottom line

The five filings support the financial foundation, business profile and fundamental credit work selected for this run, but not covenant headroom, note pricing, rating triggers or recovery, so creditor protection beyond reported covenant compliance cannot be judged from them.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 120–121; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134

The evidence is one reporting entity current to 2026-09-30: debt of USD 896 million on the balance sheet against USD 900 million of note principal, unrestricted cash of USD 328 million and a USD 700 million revolver with no borrowings outstanding. The covenant level, revolver availability after letters of credit, ratings, quotes, guarantor names and the executed debt documents are not in the set, and each limits only the conclusion that depends on it.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C02; calculation C03
### Key findings

The set is one reporting entity across five primary filings: the annual reports for 2024 and 2025 and the quarterly reports for March, June and September 2026. The newest was signed 20 days before the cutoff, so events between 2026-10-29 and 2026-11-18 are not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 46; calculation C01

The statements support a financial foundation: audited annual statements for 2023 to 2025, and for 2026 the first quarter, six months and nine months, each with income statement, balance sheet, cash flow and a reconciliation of net income to adjusted earnings. The 2025 interim periods exist only as comparatives inside the 2026 reports, so discrete 2025 quarters are not available as filed, and the quarterly worksite-employee charts in the annual report carry no figures in the text.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 93–95; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 27–29; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74

Debt instruments are identifiable: a USD 500 million senior unsecured note due March 2029, a USD 400 million senior unsecured note due August 2031, and a USD 700 million revolver with no borrowings outstanding since July 2025. None of the three facilities matures within twelve months of the cutoff, but the revolver maturity of August 2028 is stated only in the 2024 annual report. Rates, effective rates and issuance costs are printed only in the annual report. The quarterly reports give principal and the balance-sheet figure of USD 896 million but no instrument table, and the principal of USD 900 million exceeds that figure by USD 4 million without a printed explanation.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 118–119; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 126; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C02; calculation C03

Corporate liquidity can be built from the filings: unrestricted cash was USD 328 million at 2026-09-30, and the filings separate it from payroll and insurance-collateral funds that are restricted. The undrawn amount of the revolver after letters of credit is stated only at year-end, USD 699 million of USD 700 million at 2025-12-31, so the September 2026 amount is not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 21–22; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 120

Claims outside debt are identifiable and sit outside the debt figure: operating lease liabilities of USD 47 million at 2025-12-31, purchase obligations of USD 136 million, workers' compensation obligations of USD 151 million, and the payroll and tax liabilities held for worksite employees, which the filings show offset by matching client-related current assets. No pension, retiree medical, factoring, supply-chain finance or consent decree obligation is described, and litigation is accrued at amounts the filings call immaterial.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 80–81; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 118; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39

The revolver carries a financial covenant on maximum total net leverage, and compliance is stated at every period end supplied. The maximum level, any step-down, the definition and the reported ratio are not printed, so headroom is not calculable. The restrictions in the note indentures on liens, subsidiary guarantees and mergers are described only in summary.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 121; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 83

The run settings supply no ratings, quotes, deal terms, peer set, portfolio, management bridge or executed debt documents, and the filings name no rating of the issuer. Ratings & triggers, Peer benchmark, Security selection, Legal & covenants and Recovery & fulcrum therefore have no evidence in this set, and Market-implied risk has only the pricing-service fair values of the two notes.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 120–121; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 37

Ownership evidence is partial: the largest stockholder, an investment firm affiliated with Atairos, held about 38% at 2026-01-31 and keeps a board nomination right while it holds at least 15%, but directors, officers and compensation sit in a proxy statement that was not supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 62; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 2
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case against a ready-with-limitations verdict is that the missing items sit exactly where a creditor needs precision: the leverage covenant is the one maintenance test the filings mention, and the revolver is the one committed bank facility they describe. Supplying the credit agreement and indentures would let covenant headroom, availability after letters of credit, guarantee status and lien limits be tested, and Legal & covenants and Covenant capacity could move out of blocked. A filing, release or rating action dated between 2026-10-29 and 2026-11-18 could also change the view, because a later financing, amendment or acquisition would sit outside every figure in this set.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134

Consistent compliance statements in all five filings, and no revolver borrowings since July 2025, point the other way: they suggest the missing covenant level matters less to the selected modules than to a covenant or recovery analysis. They do not replace the level.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 121; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 128; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134
### Limitations

The verdicts rest on filing text only. Tables are flattened into lines, charts are not retained as figures, and a page reference in this work is a text chunk, not a printed page. Absent items are never treated as zero: the 2025 interim filings as filed, the covenant level, letters of credit at 2026-09-30, the proxy statement, every guarantor name, any filing after 2026-10-29 and every external input. The revolver maturity is stated only in the 2024 annual report. The Cocoon closing day and the 2023 adjusted EBITDA margin differ between filings and are preserved, not reconciled. File integrity and text extraction were verified before this module ran, and no result is recorded here.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 126; 10-Q_2026-03-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 43

- Material: The 2021 credit agreement and its amendments, the 2021 and 2023 indentures and the two 2025 supplemental indentures are listed as exhibits but were not supplied. Redemption prices after the call dates, lien and guarantee limits, events of default and security cannot be read from the documents themselves.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 45–46

- Material: The guarantors of the two note issues are not named, the exhibit list names TriNet USA, Inc. as Holdings under the credit agreement and refers to a separate borrower it does not name, and no obligor, restricted-group or subsidiary financials are supplied. The two supplemental indentures dated March 2025 list only the company and the trustee as parties, and the filings do not say what they changed, so guarantee status is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 119

- Material: Revolver availability after letters of credit is stated only at year-end, USD 699 million at 2025-12-31 and USD 606 million at 2024-12-31, and the 2024 annual report says letters of credit reduce availability. The amount at 2026-09-30 is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 120; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 128; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 126; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25

- Material: The run settings supply no ratings, quotes, deal terms, peer set, portfolio, management bridge, prior case or executed legal documents, and the filings give no rating of the issuer. Ratings & triggers, Peer benchmark, Security selection, Legal & covenants and Recovery & fulcrum have no evidence in this set; Market-implied risk has only pricing-service fair values of the notes.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 120–121; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 37

- Minor: Nothing dated after 2026-10-29 was supplied: no earnings release, current report, rating action or market price. Events up to the cutoff are not established beyond the October dividend recorded in the latest quarterly report.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10

- Minor: The proxy statement incorporated by reference into the annual report was not supplied, so directors, officers, compensation and the beneficial ownership table are not established; Atairos's holding is taken from a risk factor as at 2026-01-31.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 62

- Minor: The revolver maturity of 2028-08-16 is stated only in the 2024 annual report. The 2025 annual report and the 2026 quarterly reports describe the revolver without restating the date, and the glossary shows no amendment later than August 2023, so the date is carried forward but not reconfirmed.
Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 126; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 2

- Minor: The first quarter report gives April 8, 2026 as the closing day of the Cocoon acquisition and the second and third quarter reports give April 10, 2026. The later reports control and the difference is kept, not reconciled; the price of USD 23 million, USD 22 million net of cash acquired, agrees across them.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-03-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 40; 10-Q_2026-06-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 43

Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; calculation C06

- Minor: The 2025 quarterly reports were not supplied, so discrete 2025 quarters exist only as comparatives inside the 2026 reports, which say some prior-year amounts were reclassified. The quarterly worksite-employee charts in the annual report carry no figures in the extracted text.

## Request

Financial foundation for Trinet Group, Inc. (tnet-937098) as of 2026-11-18 under the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the consolidated income statement, cash flow, balance sheet, debt, liquidity and credit metrics for FY2023 to FY2025, nine months 2025 and nine months 2026, with a last-twelve-months view to 2026-09-30.
## Sources
| Source | Document | Document date | sha256 | Use |

| 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K of Trinet Group, Inc. for the year ended December 31, 2024 | 2025-02-13 | dff167df35fa6c58c40fa71f75e3c029e4dffbe00c50d576f833e1f71a7bf55f | FY2023 balance sheet, FY2024 and FY2023 statements, FY2024 debt note, 2024 revolver history and remaining capacity. |

| 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K of Trinet Group, Inc. for the year ended December 31, 2025 | 2026-02-12 | fc4faff14384e279442e1e94ba41397be8676b8f8e22ba0a9628e4f56eda5fad | Audited FY2025, FY2024 and FY2023 statements, adjusted EBITDA reconciliation, debt note, liquidity and obligations. |

| 10-Q_2026-03-31_tnet.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q of Trinet Group, Inc. for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 | 2026-04-30 | 2ee0c1102c38824a525b1c7ffdd1045842db8658f75984b4a0d3e8aecf5ba2a7 | Covenant compliance statement and Cocoon acquisition notice; no figures extracted into the tables. |

| 10-Q_2026-06-30_tnet.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q of Trinet Group, Inc. for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 | 2026-07-30 | d3b010931f56e186b4bd36b7941bb66993a25a2b2c5ef5568f6b42fc2b810e4f | Cocoon acquisition note and covenant compliance statement; no figures extracted into the tables. |

| 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q of Trinet Group, Inc. for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 | 2026-10-29 | 129ed71c15bd0c1c63080ef0d5fa30243e90f8ad32a531be35d324b779874a81 | Nine-month 2026 and 2025 statements, balance sheet at 2026-09-30, capital resources, fair values and dividends. |
| Supplied analysis | Module | sha256 | Use |

| Source readiness | CP-0 | f5028dbe62ed6410c33b94be43bfb8a1f025f14edc3c98bf19335e8de4c6c6d3 | Source inventory, period fit, the covenant, letters-of-credit and legal-document gaps and the Cocoon closing-day conflict; no financial balances imported. |
Document dates are the dates on each report's signature page. No external sources were used. The run settings are not issuer evidence and are not listed.
## Findings
### Bottom line

Trinet's leverage is moderate and well covered but sits on a shrinking, interest-income-supported earnings base: net debt is 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, cash interest cover is 7.33x and no borrowed debt matures before 2029, so debt service looks secure while earnings durability is the exposure.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C09; calculation C10

Reported EBITDA of USD 359 million is derived, because the issuer states only Adjusted EBITDA of USD 460 million, and interest income on client funds supplies USD 53 million of it. Net debt of USD 568 million becomes USD 581 million, or 1.62x, after the October dividend. The covenant level and revolver availability after letters of credit are not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation C02; calculation C07; calculation C11; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Key findings

Leverage rose from FY2023 to FY2025 because earnings fell, not because debt rose, and has partly reversed in 2026: total debt fell from USD 1,093 million at FY2023 to USD 896 million at 2026-09-30, but reported EBITDA fell from USD 613 million in FY2023 to USD 339 million in FY2025 before recovering to USD 359 million on a last-twelve-months basis. Net debt over reported EBITDA moved from 1.31x to 1.72x, 1.79x and 1.58x, and on Adjusted EBITDA from 1.16x to 1.23x. Net debt counts unrestricted cash only, so the USD 50 million of corporate investments at 2026-09-30 would lower net leverage to 1.44x if included.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 93–94; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C08; calculation C09; calculation C10; calculation C14

Cash interest cover has fallen from the FY2023 level because the first coupon on the 2031 notes was paid in February 2024, after that year-end: reported EBITDA covered cash interest paid 24.52x in FY2023, 6.15x in FY2024, 6.52x in FY2025 and 7.33x on a last-twelve-months basis (9.39x on Adjusted EBITDA). Cash interest paid was USD 52 million in FY2025 and USD 49 million over the last twelve months, which compares with interest expense, bank fees and other of USD 56 million in FY2025.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 93; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 95; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 119; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation C03; calculation C10

Cash generation is solid but is returned to shareholders in full: operating cash flow was USD 303 million in FY2025 and free cash flow after capital expenditure USD 234 million, against buybacks and dividends of USD 235 million. In the nine months to 2026-09-30 free cash flow was USD 243 million against USD 134 million of buybacks and dividends, so the 2026 pace leaves room to build cash.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation C12; calculation C13

Liquidity is ample against a maturity profile with nothing borrowed due before 2029: unrestricted cash was USD 328 million and the USD 700 million revolver had no borrowings at 2026-09-30, while the only maturities are USD 500 million in 2029 and USD 400 million in 2031 and the revolver itself matures in 2028. Availability after letters of credit is stated only at year-end, USD 699 million at 2025-12-31, so the September figure is before letters of credit.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 120; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 118–119; calculation C08

Claims outside the debt figure are identifiable: operating lease liabilities of USD 67 million at 2026-09-30, purchase obligations of USD 136 million and workers' compensation obligations of USD 151 million at FY2025, none of which is added to debt. No pension, retiree medical, factoring, supply-chain finance or consent decree obligation is described, and litigation is accrued at amounts the filings call immaterial.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 80–81; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; calculation C23

The latest quarter was weaker than the nine months suggest: in Q3 2026 revenue was USD 1,175 million against USD 1,232 million, derived reported EBITDA USD 68 million against USD 79 million, Adjusted EBITDA USD 89 million against USD 100 million and net income USD 31 million against USD 34 million. The nine-month gain in Adjusted EBITDA includes a one-time recovery of USD 21 million of prior-year costs in Q2 2026, so the underlying trend is flatter than the nine-month comparison. No debt was issued or repaid in the nine months.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 27–28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation C01

Part of reported EBITDA is yield on client funds, not operations. Interest income earned on funds held for clients is booked in revenue and was USD 67 million in FY2025, or 19.76% of reported EBITDA, and USD 53 million over the last twelve months, or 14.76%. The funding float behind it is shrinking: payroll tax liabilities and other payroll withholdings fell from USD 1,906 million at FY2024 to USD 1,198 million at 2026-09-30, and nine-month interest income fell from USD 53 million to USD 39 million. Lower client balances or lower short-term rates cut EBITDA without any change in operating performance.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 93–94; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 27–28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C15; calculation C16

One subsequent event is stated: the October 2026 dividend, which was declared and unpaid at 2026-09-30 at USD 13 million. It raises net debt to USD 581 million and net leverage to 1.62x on the same reported EBITDA, and it is kept out of the period figures.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C11

Data quality limits the foundation in three ways. The issuer states no unadjusted EBITDA, so reported EBITDA is derived from income before tax, interest expense, bank fees and other, and amortization of intangible assets. The quarterly reports print no debt table, so USD 900 million of note principal exceeds balance-sheet debt of USD 896 million by USD 4 million without a printed explanation. Source dashes are carried as not supplied, not as zero.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; calculation C01; calculation C19
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case against the earnings-durability concern is nine-month momentum: Adjusted EBITDA for nine months 2026 was USD 403 million against USD 368 million a year earlier, operating cash flow rose to USD 317 million from USD 242 million, the insurance cost ratio fell to 86% from 90%, and net leverage on reported EBITDA improved from 1.79x at FY2025 to 1.58x. Implied Q4 2025 reported EBITDA was only USD 31 million, so a Q4 2026 above that level lifts the last-twelve-months figure. That case is weaker than it looks, because the nine-month gain includes the one-time recovery and the latest quarter went the other way.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; calculation C09; calculation C10; calculation C22; calculation C01

What would change the view is a reversal in the drivers of that improvement: a higher insurance cost ratio, a further fall in worksite employees (total worksite employees were down 11% year on year at 2026-09-30), lower interest income as client balances or rates fall, or shareholder payments above free cash flow as in FY2025. A covenant level or letters-of-credit figure that proved tight would also change it, and neither is in the sources.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C12; calculation C13
### Limitations

Reported EBITDA is a derived figure and the interim tables use a last-twelve-months construction, so neither ties to a printed statement line for interim periods. Debt detail by instrument is printed only at year-end, revolver availability after letters of credit is stated only at year-end, the covenant level is not printed, and discrete 2025 quarters are available only as comparatives inside the 2026 reports. Dashes in the statements are not assumed to be zero, and the October dividend is linked to the declared-and-unpaid amount by inference.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 118–120; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 32; Source readiness (CP-0)

## Findings
### Bottom line

Trinet is a co-employment HR outsourcer that earns an insurance spread on a shrinking client base, with a concentrated largest stockholder and a 2023 debt-funded buyback, so creditor governance risk is medium and rests on board discretion, not on terms we can read.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 28–29; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 62; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 88; Source readiness (CP-0)

Insurance service revenues were 84.31% of FY2025 revenue, and had the insurance cost ratio stayed at its FY2023 level, FY2025 insurance costs would have been USD 273.09 million lower, close to the USD 272 million fall in Adjusted EBITDA since FY2023. Shareholder payments of USD 235 million in FY2025 equalled free cash flow of USD 234 million. Legal capacity to distribute more is not established because the debt documents were not supplied.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 93; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C11; calculation C03
### Key findings

Earnings are an insurance-underwriting spread, so claims costs, not service fees, decide creditor cash flow. Insurance service revenues were USD 4,224 million in FY2025 against insurance costs of USD 3,835 million, and fees are set in advance, so each percentage point of the insurance cost ratio is worth USD 42.24 million of earnings. The ratio rose from 84% in FY2023 to 91% in FY2025 and was 86% in the nine months to 2026-09-30, helped by repricing and a one-time USD 21 million recovery of prior-year costs.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; calculation C08; calculation C02

The client base is shrinking and can leave quickly, so revenue visibility is short. Total worksite employees at 2026-09-30 were 10.99% below a year earlier, mainly in technology and professional services clients and partly because of health benefit repricing. PEO clients may cancel on 30 days' notice, and five states account for about 64% of paid wages, which also concentrates insurance pricing. Revenue per co-employed worksite employee rose 8%, which has so far only partly offset lost volume.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 39; calculation C06

Client funds give the business liquidity and a yield but also a contingent exposure. Clients prefund payroll, payroll taxes and benefits, which are held as restricted funds, and interest on those funds was USD 67 million of FY2025 revenue, partly from interest on payroll tax refunds. In nine months 2026 interest income was USD 39 million against USD 53 million, because of lower refund interest and lower average cash balances. In some states a PEO must pay wages and taxes even when a client has not remitted, so the prefunding discipline is a creditor protection worth monitoring.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 35

Governance risk is medium because the one documented extraction-style act is old and the current pattern is cash-funded, while capacity is unreadable. The largest stockholder, an affiliate of Atairos, held about 38% at 2026-01-31, may nominate a director while it holds 15% or more, and with directors and officers controls about 39%. In 2023 the company bought USD 360 million of shares from Atairos and USD 640 million through a tender offer, funded with USD 400 million of 2031 notes and a USD 200 million revolver draw, which lifted debt by USD 597 million in a year.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case for lower risk is that the 2023 episode has been unwound in substance: the revolver was repaid in full by July 2025 with USD 110 million in 2024 and USD 90 million in 2025, all remaining debt is two fixed-rate notes, no sponsor fees or related-party leakage are stated, related-party revenue is USD 4 million, and buybacks since then came from cash flow. A medium level would fall to low if the debt documents showed tight limits on distributions, and would rise to high if another debt-funded repurchase, a large special dividend or a stockholder fee appeared, or if the largest stockholder sold or bought a block.

### Overall governance view

Overall, Trinet presents medium sponsor and governance risk. The key supported behavior is a debt-funded repurchase of USD 1,000 million in 2023, including USD 360 million bought from the largest stockholder, which matters because it raised leverage and set the 2031 maturity and implies that the board will lever for repurchases when it judges the price right. Countervailing evidence is a repaid revolver, buybacks funded from cash flow since, no stockholder fees stated and clean audit opinions. Further analysis requires the credit agreement, the indentures and the proxy statement. Governance review completed with limitations; the risk level is medium and the key gaps are the debt documents and the proxy statement.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Trinet is adequate for creditors near term but exposed on earnings: debt service is well covered and nothing borrowed matures before 2029, yet earnings are an insurance spread on a shrinking client base, so repayment depends on claims discipline.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

Net debt of USD 568 million was 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA at 2026-09-30, and USD 581 million or 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, with cash interest cover of 7.33x. Free cash flow equalled shareholder payments in FY2025, so net debt falls only while buybacks stay below free cash flow. Covenant headroom is not established.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01; calculation C18
### Key findings

Debt service capacity is strong and the maturity profile is clean, but the first test is the sequence of refinancing. Net debt of USD 568 million is 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA of USD 359 million, or USD 581 million and 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, and cash interest cover is 7.33x. Both notes are fixed rate and senior unsecured, and the first maturity is USD 500 million in March 2029. The USD 700 million revolver has no borrowings but matures in August 2028, before those notes, so it must be extended or replaced to remain a backstop when the notes turn current; its maturity date is stated only in the 2024 annual report.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 126; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01

Earnings are the weakest dimension because they are an insurance spread, not a service fee. Adjusted EBITDA fell from USD 697 million in FY2023 to USD 425 million in FY2025, a fall of 39.02%, while the insurance cost ratio rose from 84% to 91%, and each point of that ratio is worth USD 42.24 million on FY2025 insurance service revenues. The ratio of 86% for the nine months to 2026-09-30 includes a one-time recovery of USD 21 million, the third quarter ratio was 89%, Adjusted EBITDA in the third quarter was USD 89 million against USD 100 million a year earlier and the last-twelve-months ratio was 88.29%, so the recovery to USD 460 million of last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA is not yet a trend.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 93; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 11; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C03; calculation C16; calculation C04

Revenue durability is weak because the client base is shrinking and can leave on short notice. Total worksite employees were 10.99% below a year earlier at 2026-09-30, mainly in technology and professional services clients and partly because of health benefit repricing, and total revenues fell 4.86% in the nine months despite 8% higher monthly revenue per worksite employee. Clients can generally cancel on 30 days' notice, and five states account for about 64% of paid wages, which concentrates both revenue and insurance pricing. No client exceeded 10% of revenue in 2023 to 2025 and bad debt was USD 3 million a year, so the risk is broad attrition, not the loss of one large client.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 112; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C15

Cash conversion is good, but shareholder payments, not operations, decide whether leverage falls. Free cash flow was USD 234 million in FY2025 against shareholder payments of USD 235 million, and USD 243 million against USD 134 million in the nine months to 2026-09-30, so payments took 100.43% of free cash flow in FY2025 and 55.14% in 2026. The board added USD 336 million of repurchase authority in February 2026 and USD 311 million remained at 2026-09-30, and the revolver's limits on payments to stockholders cannot be read, so the pace is a board choice that no readable term constrains.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 83; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 24; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C18

A material part of reported EBITDA is yield on client funds, and it is running off. Interest income was 19.76% of FY2025 reported EBITDA and 14.76% over the last twelve months, and it fell to USD 39 million in the nine months to 2026-09-30 from USD 53 million because refund interest and average balances fell. Receivables from the IRS for employee retention credits fell from USD 831 million at FY2024 to USD 310 million at 2026-09-30, so part of the shrinking client balances is refunds being processed, not clients leaving, which qualifies the Financial foundation's reading of the fall as a shrinking funding float; the filings do not say how much. If the IRS finds claims ineligible, Trinet may seek reimbursement from clients, to whom a net USD 21 million had been distributed at 2026-09-30, but the annual report says the IRS holds professional employer organizations responsible for repaying rejected tax credits and a contract does not guarantee recovery from clients.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 48; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 108; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 27; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 34; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C01; calculation C14

Liquidity is adequate near term, with one exposure that a bad insurance year would call on twice. Unrestricted cash was USD 328 million at 2026-09-30, and pro forma cash after the October 2026 dividend is not established. The USD 700 million revolver was undrawn before letters of credit, while USD 299 million of carrier collateral sits in restricted funds and carriers may require it to be adjusted when facts change, and Trinet says it anticipates funding further collateral. A claims shock would therefore lower EBITDA and could also pull corporate cash into collateral.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 80; calculation C02

Governance risk is medium and rests on willingness, not on terms a creditor can read. In 2023 the company repurchased about USD 1,000 million of shares, USD 360 million of them from the largest stockholder, which holds about 38% and may nominate a director, using USD 600 million of new borrowings; since then the revolver has been repaid and buybacks have come from cash flow. The debt documents and the proxy statement were not supplied, so the limits on future payments and the board's independence are not established.

Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 88; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 126; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 62; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 83; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 115; Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

Refinancing the 2029 notes will probably cost more but looks manageable. The notes carry 3.50%, and the pricing-service fair value of USD 467 million against USD 500 million of principal, 93.40% of principal, indicates a market yield above that coupon, while the 2031 notes fell from USD 414 million to USD 397 million of fair value against USD 400 million of principal. If the 2029 notes were refinanced at the coupon of the 2031 notes, cash interest cover would fall from 7.33x to 5.35x on last-twelve-months reported EBITDA; this is an assumption, not a market quote.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 37; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C13; calculation C11; calculation C12
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case against the earnings concern is the 2026 recovery: nine-month operating cash flow was USD 317 million against USD 242 million, the insurance cost ratio was 86% against 90%, management calls the reset of health benefit rates substantially complete, and net debt was 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA against 1.79x at FY2025, with USD 581 million and 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend. If the ratio holds between 86% and 89% for four more quarters while worksite employees stabilise, earnings stability would move from weak to average and leverage would fall without a change in policy. The case is weaker than it looks: the nine-month ratio includes the USD 21 million one-time recovery, the third quarter ratio was 89%, USD 43 million of the USD 75 million rise in operating cash flow came from smaller working-capital outflows that can reverse, and the client base was still 10.99% smaller than a year earlier.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01; calculation C19

The view would weaken if the insurance cost ratio returned to the FY2025 level of 91% from the 88.29% implied for the last twelve months: that is worth USD 111 million, or 30.92% of last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, and would take net leverage to 2.29x, or 2.34x on USD 581 million pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, and cash interest cover to 5.06x before any repricing offset. It would also weaken if shareholder payments exceeded free cash flow again, if carrier collateral rose above USD 299 million, if the revolver were drawn, or if another debt-funded repurchase appeared. It would strengthen if the debt documents showed tight limits on payments to stockholders, or if the covenant level and letters of credit showed wide headroom.
Basis: calculation C04; calculation C05; calculation C07; calculation C08; calculation C02
### Limitations

- No peer set, rating or market quote was supplied, so the business profile is not compared with other issuers and the adequacy conclusion rests on the issuer's own history; a peer comparison could move the assessment of earnings stability in either direction.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)

- The sensitivity of leverage and cover to the insurance cost ratio applies a return to 91% to last-twelve-months insurance service revenues and ignores repricing, tax relief and further client losses, so it shows scale, not a forecast; it would overstate the fall if rates rise with claims and understate it if client losses continue.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 93; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation C04; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C07; calculation C08

- The refinancing illustration assumes the 2029 notes are replaced at the coupon of the 2031 notes, which is not a market yield; with no yield supplied, the cost of refinancing could be materially higher or lower, and the view on market access is qualitative.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 37; calculation C11; calculation C12

- The share of the fall in client balances that is refund processing rather than client departures is not stated, so the conclusion that interest income is running off is an inference and its pace is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 108; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 34; calculation C14
- The amount of carrier collateral that could be called in a bad claims year is not stated, so the liquidity conclusion holds only while collateral stays near the current level.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 80; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 35
### Strengths and weaknesses

The strongest support is low, fixed-rate leverage with a distant first maturity. Net debt of USD 568 million is 1.58x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, or USD 581 million and 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, all debt is two unsecured fixed-rate notes, and the first maturity is USD 500 million in March 2029. Rate rises do not lift interest cost while the revolver is undrawn, and an earnings shock has more than two years before a refinancing, which lowers the probability of default over that period.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; Financial foundation (CP-1)

A second support is cash conversion. Free cash flow was USD 286 million over the last twelve months after USD 49 million of cash interest, so debt service is covered comfortably and leverage can fall quickly if buybacks slow, which supports deleveraging capacity.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01

A third support is that client money does not fund the company. Clients prefund payroll and related taxes, and the USD 941 million of payroll funds collected and USD 40 million held in the trust for administrative services users at 2026-09-30 are restricted and matched by liabilities to clients and tax authorities, so working capital does not draw on corporate cash and the USD 328 million of unrestricted cash is available for debt service; pro forma cash after the October 2026 dividend is not established.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 21–22; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 35; Source readiness (CP-0); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01

A fourth support is a simpler structure. The revolver was repaid in 2024 and 2025, the two notes are the only debt, and the 2023 debt-funded repurchase has not been repeated, which removes floating-rate exposure and leaves the next test to 2028 and 2029.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 83; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 115; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 119; Business & governance (CP-1A)

The weakest dimension is earnings stability. Adjusted EBITDA fell USD 272 million from FY2023 to FY2025 as the insurance cost ratio rose from 84% to 91%, and each point is worth USD 42.24 million, so a return to the FY2025 ratio would remove USD 111 million, or 30.92%, of last-twelve-months reported EBITDA, and fees fixed in advance leave no time to react.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C03; calculation C05; calculation C16

A second weakness is a shrinking client base with short contracts. Total worksite employees were 10.99% lower year on year, clients can cancel on 30 days' notice, and the repricing that lifts margin contributed to the losses, so revenue has to be won back at the same time as margin is defended.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; Business & governance (CP-1A)

A third weakness is that shareholder payments absorb free cash flow at the board's discretion. Payments of USD 235 million matched free cash flow of USD 234 million in FY2025, the largest stockholder holds about 38%, and the limits in the debt documents are not readable, so leverage is a policy variable, not a result.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 62; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C18

A fourth weakness is that part of EBITDA is yield on client funds. Interest income was 19.76% of FY2025 reported EBITDA and fell to USD 39 million from USD 53 million in nine months, so lower client balances or short-term rates reduce EBITDA without any change in operations.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 93; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 27; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01

### Source readiness and scope

Fundamental credit is ready with limitations. Five filings of one reporting entity, current to 2026-09-30, and the earlier Source readiness, Financial foundation and Business & governance work support the view; ratings, market quotes, a peer set, executed debt documents, the proxy statement and anything dated after 2026-10-29 were not supplied, so covenant headroom, guarantor status, recovery and relative value sit outside it.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 46; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Company and ownership

Trinet is a co-employment professional employer organization and administrative services provider for small and medium-size businesses, and its cash flow follows insurance claims experience more than service volume. Insurance service revenues were 84.31% of FY2025 revenue and are billed at rates set before the benefit period, professional service fees are paid per worksite employee, and interest is earned on client funds. Prefunding by clients supports liquidity, but claims arrive after the price is fixed and clients can leave on 30 days' notice, so cash-flow visibility is short.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 9–10; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74; Business & governance (CP-1A)

Control rests on board discretion rather than on terms a creditor can read. An Atairos affiliate holds about 38% and may nominate a director while it holds 15% or more, and directors and officers with affiliates hold about 39% in total. In 2023 the company repurchased about USD 1,000 million of shares with USD 600 million of new borrowings, which lifted debt by USD 597 million in the year; the revolver was repaid by July 2025. The guarantors of the notes and the revolver borrower are not named, so how the notes rank against claims at operating subsidiaries, including client-fund and carrier obligations, is not established.

Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 88; 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 126; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 62; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 115; Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)
### Revenue durability

Revenue is recurring in form but falling in practice. Professional service revenues were 14.11% and insurance service revenues 84.80% of nine-month 2026 revenue, and both follow volume: total worksite employees fell 10.99% year on year and nine-month revenue fell 4.86%, with 8% higher monthly revenue per worksite employee offsetting only part of the loss. Clients showed modest staffing reductions in every vertical in 2025 and net hiring was low, so same-client volume is not a source of growth. Revenue will keep falling unless attrition slows, and repricing that lifts revenue per employee may itself feed attrition, which management links to the technology and professional services losses.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C15

Revenue visibility is short and concentrated. PEO clients renew annually but may cancel on 30 days' notice, administrative services clients are monthly or annual on the same notice, and five states account for about 64% of paid wages. No client exceeded 10% of revenue in 2023 to 2025 and bad debt net of recoveries was USD 3 million in each year, so concentration in single clients is small, but revenue by vertical and client size is not disclosed and the breadth of attrition is not established.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 112; Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Margin resilience

Margins are fragile to claims experience and only partly flexible on cost. Insurance costs were USD 3,835 million of USD 4,793 million total costs and expenses in FY2025, and because fees are set ahead of claims a rise in the insurance cost ratio falls straight through to earnings, as the move from 84% to 91% did. The Adjusted EBITDA margin fell from about 14% in FY2023 to 8.48% in FY2025 and was 9.53% over the last twelve months; the FY2023 margin is printed as 14.2% in one annual report and 14.0% in the other. Operating expenses of USD 902 million carry the cost flexibility: restructuring costs of USD 49 million in 2024, USD 11 million in 2025 and USD 13 million in nine months 2026 show that management can resize costs, but savings are not quantified, so margin recovery rests mainly on repricing and claims, not cost.

Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 70; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 129–130; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 41; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)
### Cash conversion

Capital intensity is low and cash conversion is high, but part of the 2026 improvement is timing. Capital expenditures including capitalized software were USD 69 million in FY2025 and USD 74 million in nine months 2026 against USD 51 million a year earlier, and free cash flow was USD 234 million in FY2025 and USD 286 million over the last twelve months after cash interest of USD 49 million. Of the USD 75 million rise in nine-month operating cash flow to USD 317 million, USD 43 million came from smaller working-capital outflows, which can reverse. Free cash flow comfortably covers debt service but is not a clean measure of recurring capacity, and with no printed split between maintenance and growth capital spending, flexibility over the maturity wall is not measured.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C01; calculation C19
### Competitive forces

Rivalry is intense and caps repricing. Direct competitors include large professional employer organizations such as the units of ADP, Paychex and Insperity and many smaller providers, and Trinet's offer must be priced competitively with what clients can buy themselves, so recovering margin through rate rises risks the client losses already seen.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10

The threat of new entrants is moderate. Payroll agents, other human capital providers and insurance brokers that integrate third-party HR systems can offer parts of the service, and the administrative services offer, where Trinet does not co-employ, competes with a wider field; the filings describe state insurance licensing as complex, which is a barrier mainly for the core PEO offer.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 22

The threat of substitutes is real. Companies can run payroll, benefits and HR in-house or through payroll processors, and clients may buy insurance through brokers, so the benefit-scale advantage has to stay visible in price; substitution would show first as worksite employee attrition, already 10.99% year on year.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 13; Business & governance (CP-1A)

Buyer power is high at the margin. Small and medium-size clients can cancel on 30 days' notice, were cutting staff in 2025 and can compare offers, so price increases meet low switching cost and weak revenue visibility.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18

Supplier power sits with insurance carriers. Trinet relies on carriers for health and workers' compensation cover, carriers set the fixed cost of guaranteed-cost plans, about 88% of group health costs are risk-based plans in which Trinet reimburses claims within a deductible layer, and carriers set collateral. A change in carrier terms or a loss of a key carrier is therefore a direct credit event for margin and for restricted cash.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 80; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 86; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 104
### External factors

Economic and regulatory factors are material to credit; social and technological factors do not appear to be a primary credit driver based on the provided materials. Net hiring by small and medium-size clients was low in 2025 and short-term interest rates fell, which cuts interest income on client funds and would lower the cost of any revolver borrowing, so the net rate effect is negative for earnings and mildly positive for debt cost. The IRS is examining some employee retention credit claims filed for clients, Trinet may seek reimbursement from clients if claims are found ineligible but the IRS holds professional employer organizations responsible for repaying rejected credits and a contract does not guarantee recovery, and state insurance licensing and benefit rules apply; an adverse finding or fine would hit cash directly, but no amount is stated.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 48; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 108; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 34
### SWOT

Strengths in credit terms are low fixed-rate leverage, a distant first maturity, strong cash conversion and prefunded client money. Weaknesses are an insurance-spread earnings base, a shrinking client base, shareholder payments at the level of free cash flow and a part of EBITDA that is yield on client funds.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

The opportunities that could improve credit quality are completed repricing that holds the insurance cost ratio near its 2026 level, stabilising worksite employees through the broker channel and new software and leave-management tools, and lower interest cost on any future revolver use as short-term rates fall. The threats that could weaken it are health cost inflation and utilisation, further client losses, an adverse IRS finding on retention credit claims, a debt-funded repurchase and carrier collateral calls.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 34
### Financial profile and credit quality

The financial profile is adequate: strong on leverage, liquidity and cash conversion, weak on earnings stability, and not assessable for covenant headroom. Net debt of USD 568 million is 1.58x reported EBITDA, or USD 581 million and 1.62x pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, cash interest cover is 7.33x and unrestricted cash at 2026-09-30, before the October 2026 dividend, covers 65.60% of the 2029 notes, but Adjusted EBITDA of USD 460 million is USD 237 million below FY2023 and interest income is part of earnings. Since FY2023 debt fell from USD 1,093 million to USD 896 million while reported EBITDA fell from USD 613 million to USD 339 million in FY2025 before USD 359 million over the last twelve months, so the trend is lower earnings on lower debt. The data most needed to firm the view are the covenant level, letters of credit, the debt documents, the proxy statement and a peer set.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; Financial foundation (CP-1); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation C01; calculation C17; calculation C20
### Outlook

Over twelve to twenty-four months the insurance cost ratio decides the outcome. Management says the reset of health benefit rates is substantially complete, the ratio was 86% in nine months and 89% in the third quarter, and claims costs rise later in the year, so the last-twelve-months figure will move with the fourth quarter, when the implied 2025 ratio was 94.18% against 89.65% for the first nine months and implied Adjusted EBITDA was only USD 57 million against USD 368 million. Interest income is likely to keep falling with client balances and rates, and the filings give no quantified outlook for worksite employees or earnings. No debt matures, but the revolver's August 2028 maturity falls inside the window and the 2029 notes turn current in early 2028.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 71; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C21

Over three to five years the credit is a question of policy and refinancing. USD 500 million falls due in March 2029 and USD 400 million in August 2031, and a refinancing of the 2029 notes at a higher coupon would raise interest cost. With moderate leverage and free cash flow, refinancing capacity looks adequate if earnings hold, but it will depend on the leverage the board allows through buybacks, the insurance cost ratio and the worksite employee trend at the time. Sector tailwinds are the scale advantage in benefits for small businesses and lower short-term rates on revolver cost; headwinds are health cost inflation, low small-business hiring and competition from larger providers.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 26; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 19; Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Downside scenario

The issuer-specific downside is a claims shock layered on continued client losses. The initiating condition is health utilisation above the rates fixed for the plan year, as in 2024 and 2025, and the first operational break is the insurance cost ratio rising while worksite employees keep falling, because fees cannot be reset until the next benefit period. The ratio implied for the last twelve months is 88.29%, and the fourth quarter is the seasonal weak point: the implied FY2025 fourth-quarter ratio was 94.18% against 89.65% for the first nine months. If the ratio returned to the FY2025 level of 91%, the extra insurance cost on last-twelve-months insurance service revenues would be USD 111 million, which would cut reported EBITDA from USD 359 million to USD 248 million and Adjusted EBITDA from USD 460 million to USD 349 million before any repricing offset.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 93; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 74; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 11; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C04; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C21

The financial transmission is meaningful but is not a solvency event. Net debt of USD 568 million would be 2.29x the reduced reported EBITDA, or 2.34x on USD 581 million pro forma for the October 2026 dividend, and cash interest cover would fall to 5.06x. Free cash flow would fall to USD 175 million before tax relief, which still covers dividends of USD 52 million 3.37x but leaves USD 123 million for buybacks against USD 183 million in FY2025. Carrier collateral could draw on liquidity as well, since USD 299 million is held now and carriers may require more. Nothing matures before 2029, so resilience appears sufficient to avoid a liquidity event even if buybacks continue at a reduced pace and the revolver stays available, but leverage would not stay at present levels while paying shareholders as in FY2025, and a larger or longer rise in claims or further client losses would take it well beyond this sensitivity.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 28; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 80; 10-K_2025-12-31_tnet.htm.jsonl, pages 94–95; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C07; calculation C08; calculation C09; calculation C10; calculation C02

Management levers are stopping buybacks, which were USD 94 million in nine months 2026, further repricing, restructuring and revolver use of up to USD 700 million before letters of credit. The observable triggers are a quarterly insurance cost ratio above the same quarter a year earlier, when the fourth quarter ran at an implied 94.18% and the third quarter at 90%, worksite employees below their latest level, collateral balances above USD 299 million, any revolver borrowing and a debt-funded repurchase.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-Q_2026-09-30_tnet.htm.jsonl, page 35; calculation C02; calculation C21
### Overall credit view

Overall, Trinet presents an adequate business profile supported by scale in small-business HR outsourcing, with total revenues of USD 5,010 million in FY2025, an operating record since 1988 and prefunded client money, but credit quality is constrained by an insurance-spread earnings base, a shrinking client base and shareholder payments at the level of free cash flow. No peer set was supplied, so the comparison with typical leveraged-credit issuers in the sector is not established. Cash-flow durability appears adequate for debt service, because capital spending is modest and debt is low and fixed rate, but weak as a measure of recurring earnings, because the insurance cost ratio and client losses can remove a large share of EBITDA within a year. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on the insurance cost ratio and worksite employee trend at the time, the leverage the board allows through buybacks, and the extension of the revolver before it matures in August 2028. The primary downside path is claims costs rising above rates set in advance while clients leave, with cash drawn into carrier collateral and shareholder payments continuing. Further analysis would require the credit agreement and indentures, the covenant level, letters of credit outstanding, the proxy statement, a peer set and market quotes. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: the insurance cost ratio.
